In [[algebraic number theory]], the '''conductor''' of a [[finite extension|finite]] [[abelian extension]] of [[local field|local]] or [[global field]]s provides a quantitative measure of the [[Ramification (mathematics)|ramification]] in the extension. The definition of the conductor is related to the [[Artin map]].

==Local conductor==
Let <math>L/K</math> be a finite abelian extension of [[non-Archimedean local field]]s. The '''conductor''' of <math>L/K</math>, denoted <math>\mathfrak{f}(L/K)</math>, is the smallest non-negative [[integer]] <math>n</math> such that the [[higher unit group]] 
:<math>U^{(n)} = 1 + \mathfrak{m}_K^n = \left\{u\in\mathcal{O}^\times: u \equiv 1\, \left(\operatorname{mod} \mathfrak{m}_K^n\right)\right\}</math>

is contained in <math>N_{L/K}(L^\times)</math>, where <math>N_{L/K}</math> is [[field norm]] map and <math>\mathfrak{m}_K</math> is the [[local field|maximal ideal]] of <math>K</math>.{{sfnp|Serre|1967|loc=§4.2}} Equivalently, <math>n</math> is the smallest integer such that the [[local Artin map]] is trivial on <math>U_K^{(n)}</math>. Sometimes, the conductor is defined as <math>\mathfrak{m}_K^n</math> where <math>n</math> is as above.{{sfnp|Neukirch|1999|loc=definition V.1.6}}

The conductor of an extension measures the ramification. Qualitatively, the extension is [[unramified]] if and only if the conductor is zero,{{sfnp|Neukirch|1999|loc=proposition V.1.7}} and it is [[tamely ramified]] if and only if the conductor is 1.{{sfnp|Milne|2020|loc=I.1.9}} More precisely, the conductor computes the non-triviality of [[higher ramification group]]s: if <math>s</math> is the largest integer for which the "[[lower numbering]]" higher ramification group ''G<sub>s</sub>'' is non-trivial, then <math>\mathfrak{f}(L/K) = \eta_{L/K}(s) + 1</math>, where <math>\eta_{L/K}</math> is the function that translates from "lower numbering" to "[[upper numbering]]" of higher ramification groups.{{sfnp|Serre|1967|loc=§4.2, proposition 1}}

The conductor of <math>L/K</math> is also related to the [[Artin conductor]]s of characters of the [[Galois group]] <math>\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)</math>. Specifically,{{sfnp|Artin|Tate|2009|loc=corollary to theorem XI.14|p= 100}}
:<math>\mathfrak{m}_K^{\mathfrak{f}(L/K)} = \operatorname{lcm}\limits_\chi \mathfrak{m}_K^{\mathfrak{f}_\chi}</math>

where <math>\chi</math> varies over all [[Multiplicative character|multiplicative complex characters]] of <math>\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)</math>, <math>\mathfrak{f}_\chi</math> is the Artin conductor of <math>\chi</math>, and lcm is the [[least common multiple]].

===More general fields===
The conductor can be defined in the same way for <math>L/K</math> a not necessarily abelian finite Galois extension of local fields.{{sfnp|Serre|1967|loc=§4.2}} However, it only depends on <math>L^\mathrm{ab}/K</math>, the maximal abelian extension of <math>K</math> in <math>L</math>, because of the "norm limitation theorem", which states that, in this situation,{{sfnp|Serre|1967|loc=§2.5, proposition 4}}{{sfnp|Milne|2020|loc=theorem III.3.5}}
: <math>N_{L/K}\left(L^\times\right) = N_{L^{\text{ab}}/K} \Big(\left(L^{\text{ab}}\right)^\times \Big).</math>

Additionally, the conductor can be defined when <math>L</math> and <math>K</math> are allowed to be slightly more general than local, namely if they are [[complete valued field]]s with [[quasi-finite field|quasi-finite]] residue field.<ref>As in {{harvtxt|Artin|Tate|2009}}, §XI.4. This is the situation in which the formalism of [[local class field theory]] works.</ref>

===Archimedean fields===
Mostly for the sake of global conductors, the conductor of the trivial extension <math>\R/\R</math> is defined to be 0, and the conductor of the extension <math>\C/\R</math> is defined to be 1.{{sfnp|Cohen|2000|loc=definition 3.4.1}}

==Global conductor==

===Algebraic number fields===
The '''conductor''' of an abelian extension <math>L/K</math> of number fields can be defined, similarly to the local case, using the Artin map. Specifically, let <math>\theta: l^m\to\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)</math> be the [[global Artin map]] where the [[modulus (algebraic number theory)|modulus]] '''m''' is a [[defining modulus]] for ''L''/''K''; we say that [[Artin reciprocity law|Artin reciprocity]] holds for '''m''' if θ factors through the [[ray class group|ray class group modulo]] '''m'''. We define the conductor of <math>L/K</math>, denoted <math>\mathfrak{f}(L/K)</math>, to be the highest common factor of all moduli for which reciprocity holds; in fact reciprocity holds for <math>\mathfrak{f}(L/K)</math>, so it is the smallest such modulus.{{sfnp|Milne|2020|loc=remark V.3.8}}{{sfnp|Janusz|1996|pp=158,168–169}}<ref>Some authors omit infinite places from the conductor, see {{harvtxt|Neukirch|1999}}, §VI.6.</ref>

====Example====
*Taking as base the field of rational numbers, the [[Kronecker–Weber theorem]] states that an algebraic number field <math>K</math> is abelian over <math>\Q</math> if and only if it is a subfield of a [[cyclotomic field]] <math>\Q(\zeta_n)</math>, where <math>\zeta_n</math> denotes a primitive <math>n</math>th root of unity.{{sfnp|Manin|Panchishkin|2005|pp=155, 168}} If <math>n</math> is the smallest integer for which this holds, the conductor of <math>K</math> is then <math>n</math> if <math>K</math> is fixed by complex conjugation and <math>n \infty</math> otherwise.
* Let <math>L/K</math> be <math>\Q(\sqrt{d})/\Q</math> where <math>d</math> is a [[squarefree]] integer. Then,{{sfnp|Milne|2020|loc=example V.3.11}}
*: <math>\mathfrak{f}(\Q(\sqrt{d})/\Q) = \begin{cases}
        |\Delta_{\Q(\sqrt{d})}| & \text{for }d > 0 \\
  \infty|\Delta_{\Q(\sqrt{d})}| & \text{for }d < 0
\end{cases}</math>
: where <math>\Delta_{\Q(\sqrt{d})}</math> is the [[discriminant of an algebraic number field|discriminant]] of <math>\Q(\sqrt{d})/\Q</math>.

====Relation to local conductors and ramification====
The global conductor is the product of local conductors:<ref>For the finite part see {{harvtxt|Neukirch|1999}}, proposition VI.6.5, and for the infinite part {{harvtxt|Cohen|2000}}, definition 3.4.1.</ref>
:<math>\mathfrak{f}(L/K) = \prod_\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{p}^{\mathfrak{f}\left(L_\mathfrak{p}/K_\mathfrak{p}\right)}.</math>

As a consequence, a finite prime is ramified in <math>L/K</math> if, and only if, it divides <math>\mathfrak{f}(L/K)</math>.{{sfnp|Neukirch|1999|loc=corollary VI.6.6}} An infinite prime <math>v</math> occurs in the conductor if, and only if, <math>v</math> is real and becomes complex in <math>L</math>.
